what_its_for: This medication is a combination birth control pill that contains two hormones — a progestin (norethindrone) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol). It is mainly used to prevent pregnancy. It may also be prescribed to help with acne, painful or irregular periods, endometriosis, or to make periods lighter and more regular. Your doctor may have given it to you for one or more of these reasons.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Try to pick a time that is easy for you to remember, like when you brush your teeth in the morning or before bed. Swallow the pill whole with or without food. If the pill makes your stomach upset, taking it with food or at bedtime may help. Follow the order of pills in your pack exactly — do not skip pills or take them out of order. Some packs have reminder pills (placebo pills) at the end — take those too so you stay in the habit of taking a pill every day.
dosing: Take one tablet every day for 21 or 28 days depending on your pill pack. If you have a 21-day pack, take one pill daily for 21 days, then take no pills for 7 days, then start a new pack. If you have a 28-day pack, take one pill every day without any break and start a new pack the very next day after finishing. Your doctor will tell you which type of pack you have. Always start a new pack on time — do not wait more than 7 days between packs.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 pill: Take it as soon as you remember, even if that means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue taking the rest of the pack as usual. If you miss 2 pills in a row in Week 1 or Week 2: Take 2 pills for 2 days in a row to catch up, then continue the rest of the pack. Use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the next 7 days. If you miss 2 pills in a row in Week 3, or miss 3 or more pills in a row at any time: Throw away the rest of your current pack and start a new pack right away. Use a backup method of birth control for 7 days. You may not get your period this month — that is okay. If you skip two periods in a row, call your doctor to rule out pregnancy. When in doubt, use a backup birth control method and call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the pills away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store them in the bathroom. Keep the medication in its original packaging so you can track which pills you have taken. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused pills down the toilet — ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of them.
what_to_avoid: Do not smoke while taking this medication, especially if you are over 35 years old. Smoking greatly increases your risk of serious blood clots, stroke, and heart attack when combined with birth control pills. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may affect how this medicine works. Do not take St. John's Wort (an herbal supplement), as it can make your birth control less effective. Some medications can also make this pill less effective, including certain seizure medications, HIV medications, and some antibiotics — always tell every doctor and pharmacist about all medications, vitamins, and supplements you take. Avoid long periods of sitting or lying still (like long flights) since birth control pills can increase your risk of blood clots.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have any of these warning signs — remember the word ACHES: Abdominal pain (severe stomach pain), Chest pain or shortness of breath, Headaches that are sudden or very severe, Eye problems like blurry vision or loss of vision, Severe leg pain or swelling in one leg. Also call your doctor if you: miss two periods in a row or think you might be pregnant, have unusual vaginal bleeding or spotting that does not go away, develop yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), feel very depressed or notice big changes in your mood, have a breast lump or any unusual breast changes, or experience symptoms of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: This pill is most effective when taken every day at the same time without missing doses. For pregnancy prevention: if you start the pill on the first day of your period, it works right away. If you start it on any other day, use a backup birth control method (like condoms) for the first 7 days. For acne or period-related benefits, it may take 2 to 3 months of regular use before you notice improvement. This medication does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) — use condoms to reduce that risk.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not take this medication if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking it, stop immediately and call your doctor. Breastfeeding: This medication may reduce your milk supply and small amounts pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before using it while breastfeeding — a progestin-only pill may be a better option. Teenagers: This pill can be used by teenagers who have already started their menstrual period. It does not affect future fertility. Women over 35 who smoke: This combination pill is generally not recommended due to a high risk of blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. Women over 50 or in menopause: This pill is generally not used after menopause. Women with certain medical conditions: Tell your doctor if you have a history of blood clots, stroke, heart disease, high blood pressure, migraines with aura, liver disease, breast cancer, or diabetes — these conditions may make this pill unsafe for you.
